title: Cap. VIII: Gualtherus and Martyr — analogy, not true likeness; no novelty charge
pass_a_gloss: Will you also hear Rudolph Gualther? The sense is that Adam and Christ can be compared in this — each propagated what was his into his own. In the rest the difference is manifold, and the account of the offense or sin brought in through Adam is not the same as the benefit shown us in Christ, and so on. And a little later: a double difference seems marked in these words, so that first corrupt nature and God's grace are opposed — because Adam, from the nature-corruption he contracted in his fall, propagated sin into all posterity so we are born sinners from the mother's womb; but Christ is given us by grace so his righteousness or obedience overflows into the many, that is into all. That we are sinners and death-liable for sin we have as our own from nature; that we are made just and life-partners is God's free benefit, who imputes his Son's righteousness to us for the faith by which we grasp him. To these two Placeus adds a third, Peter Martyr on Romans 5:14 at 'who is the type of the one to come': this likeness is to be taken in the genus — all hang from Adam, all from Christ, each in his order; and as the one merited for all his own, so also the other. But in particular and as to species the difference is great. Adam brought in sin, death, and damnation; Christ righteousness, life, and grace. There is also a difference in propagation: Adam poured his evils into humans by fleshly generation; Christ by faith. So when Paul had said Adam was type of the one to come, he almost corrects: but not as the sin, so also the gift. Therefore between Adam and Christ one should set an analogy and proportion rather than true likeness. You see Placeus defending the great men's teaching against Garissoles's assault. So do not, candid reader, damn us for novelty.
pass_b_english: Does it please you also to hear Rudolph Gualther? "The sense, then, is that Adam and Christ can indeed be compared with each other in this, that each propagated into his own what was his. But in the rest there is a manifold difference, and the account of the offense or sin brought in through Adam is not the same as that of the benefit exhibited to us in Christ," and so on. And a little later: "But a double difference seems to be noted in these words, so that first corrupt Nature and the grace of God are opposed, because Adam indeed, on account of the corruption of nature which he contracted from his fall, propagated sin into all posterity, so that we are born sinners from the very womb of our mother: but Christ was given to us by grace, so that his righteousness or obedience should overflow into the many, that is, into all. Therefore that we are sinners and liable to death because of sin, we have from nature as our own: but that we have been made just and sharers of life is the free benefit of God, who imputes to us the righteousness of his Son because of the faith by which we apprehend him." To these two I will add a third, Peter Martyr, Commentary on Romans 5:14, at the words "who is the type of the one to come" (Romans 5:14): "This likeness is to be taken in the genus, that as all depend on Adam, so all depend on Christ according to their order: and that as the one has merited for all who are his, so also the other. But particularly and as to the species there is a great difference. For Adam brought in sin, death, and damnation: but Christ righteousness, life, and grace. There is also a difference in the propagation. For Adam poured his evils into men by the generation of the flesh. But Christ by faith. Therefore when Paul had said that Adam was the type of the one to come, he subjoins as if by correction: But not as the sin, so also the gift (Romans 5:15). So between Adam and Christ an analogy and proportion of a certain kind, rather than a true likeness, is to be established." You see us defending the teaching of great men against the assault of D. Garissoles. Do not therefore, I ask, candid reader, condemn us for novelty.
source_text: Placet-ne etiam audire Rodolphum Gualterum? Sensus ergo est, in hoc quidem comparari inter se posse Adamum & Christum, quod uterque quod suum erat in suos propagarit. In caeteris vero Multiplex esse discrimen, neque eandem esse rationem offensae aut peccati per Adamum invecti, & beneficii nobis in Christo exhibiti &c. & paulo post. Videtur autem duplex discrimen his verbis annotari, ut primo quidem Natura corrupta & gratia Dei opponantur, eo quod Adam quidem propter naturae corruptionem, quam ex suo lapsu contraxit, peccatum in omnes posteros propagarit, adeo ut peccatores ex ipso matris utero nascamur: Christus vero nobis ex gratia datus sit, ut eius iustitia sive obedientia in multos, id est, in omnes redundaret. Quod ergo peccatores & propter peccatum morti obnoxii sumus, hoc ex natura ceu proprium habemus: quod vero iusti & vitae consortes facti sumus, id gratuitum Dei beneficium est, qui Filii sui iustitiam nobis imputat propter fidem, qua hunc apprehendimus. His duobus tertium adiungam Petrum Martyrem Com. in Rom. 5. Vs. 14. ad verba qui est typus futuri. Similitudo haec accipienda est in genere quod sicut omnes ab Adamo, ita omnes a Christo iuxta ordinem suum pendeant: quodque quemadmodum alter meritus est suis omnibus, ita etiam alter. Sed particulariter & quoad species magnum est discrimen. Nam Adamus peccatum, mortem, & damnationem invexit: Christus vero iustitiam, vitam & gratiam. Est etiam discrimen in propagatione. Adamus enim mala sua per carnis generationem in homines transfudit. Christus autem per fidem. Ideo Paulus cum dixisset, Adamum typum fuisse futuri, quasi per correctionem subiicit. At non ut peccatum, ita & donum. Quamobrem inter Adamum & Christum potius analogia quaedam & proportio, quam vera similitudo constituenda est. Vides nos Magnorum virorum doctrinam adversus D. Garissolii impetum defendere. Noli nos igitur quaeso, candide lector, novitatis damnare.
